query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated Q235 steel, elevated temperatures accelerate the preferential dissolution of Mn‐rich sites at grain boundaries, thereby undermining passive film formation and triggering earlier, more aggressive pitting corrosion in chloride-rich environments by enhancing ionic transport and metal dissolution at these critical regions.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state with a typical ferrite–pearlite microstructure and minor Mn segregation at grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Exposure to a chloride-containing solution maintained at an elevated temperature versus the same solution maintained at room temperature.
generation.conditions: Static immersion tests in a controlled chloride-rich solution for identical durations, comparing room temperature to elevated temperature exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries, particularly those with localized Mn segregation which serve as preferential sites for corrosion attack.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures the kinetics of ionic transport and metal dissolution are enhanced. This accelerates the attack at Mn-enriched grain boundary regions, which in turn prevents the formation or stability of a protective oxide film and facilitates pitting initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed at elevated temperature will exhibit a higher corrosion current density, greater weight loss, and more abundant and deeper pitting damage (as observed by microscopy) compared to samples exposed at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel exposed in the same chloride medium at room temperature, which will show a slower onset of pitting and lower overall corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under static chloride-rich immersion conditions; variations in dynamic flow, inhibitor presence, or significant compositional heterogeneities in the steel may affect the observed behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The extent and uniformity of initial Mn segregation in Q235 steel may vary between batches; quantitative effects of temperature on the dissolution rate and passive film stability are subject to experimental variation and require careful calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical Q235 steel specimens and characterize their initial microstructure and Mn distribution using optical/SEM microscopy and EDS mapping. Divide them into two groups for immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution: one held at room temperature and the other at an elevated temperature (e.g., 80 °C). After a fixed exposure time, assess weight loss, perform potentiodynamic polarization tests, and use SEM to evaluate pitting morphology and correlate pit locations with grain boundary regions.
measurements: Electrochemical polarization curves (to extract corrosion current density)
SEM imaging of pitting and grain boundary morphologies
EDS mapping for Mn distribution before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated temperature exposure does not yield a statistically significant increase in corrosion rate (weight loss and current density) and pitting damage at Mn-rich grain boundary regions relative to room temperature, or if there is no correlation between Mn segregation and pit initiation, then the mechanistic hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: (1) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was prepared by plasma spraying on substrate of the Q235 steel, consisting of a simple FCC solid solution with Laves phase, and the coating bonded well to the substrate. (2) Elemental segregation occurred between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, and the elements Cr and Nb with high melting point were enriched between the interdendrites. This phenomenon may be due to the difference in melting point of the element and the characteristics of the plasma spraying process. (3) The coating has a microhardness of 321 HV0.5, which can effectively improve the surface hardness of the Q235 steel part. (4) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating exhibited excellent corrosion resistance in the electrochemical corrosion test of a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution comparing to previously studied coatings prepared by other processes. (5) In the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, the selective corrosion occurred on the surface of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating, while the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode, and the dendritic phase rich in Co, Ni, and Fe was protected as a cathode.

In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
